1406: The appellant was a workman in the respondent Bank. He was dismissed from service under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders on June 21, 1958. The order of dismissal was communicated to him by the employer on July 8, 1958. On July 8, 1959, he terminated the services of the appellant and served a notice on the appellant terminating his services under r.18(a). The appellant challenged the validity of the termination before the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The appellant contended that the action taken under r. 17(a) was mala fide and was not bona fide. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that there was no evidence to prove what had actually happened and therefore it considered that no inquiry should be held. The appellant applied for special leave which was granted; and that is how the matter has come up before us. The question for consideration was whether the appellant could claim protection of the Standing orders under r. 19(a) or r. 18 (a) of Standing orders. Held, that the appellant 's contention must fail. The appellant was an employee of the respondent Bank and was dismissed from the service of the Bank. The appellant did not hold any departmental enquiry against him and the action taken was not bona fides. The appellant could not claim protection of standing orders under r, 19(a), because it was not colourable exercise of power conferred on the employer. The appellant having failed to establish that there was any misconduct committed by him, the action taken by the management was justified.

5248: The assessee was a shareholder of a company. He transferred his shares to the company and received the amount in question from the company. In appeal, the Tribunal held that the gift was not valid. On reference, the High Court held that the gifts were invalid as they did not relate to the business of banking and were not taxable under section 4(1)(a) of the Act. HELD: (1) The gift in question is not invalid merely because the donees have not made any provision for the payment of the gift money or for the return of the gift. [125 B] (2) The gift was not invalid merely on the ground that the donee was not carrying on business of banking. It was also not invalid merely by reason of the fact that the donees had not made any provisions for the repayment of the gift amount. [126 C] (3) The gift being voidable under section 4 of the Act, the gift cannot be regarded as invalid merely because it relates to the business carried on by the donor. [127 D] (4) The gift is not invalid only because it relates directly to the business but is also not invalid because it does not relate to any other business. [129 F G] (6) The gift must be deemed to be invalid if it is supported either wholly or in part by consideration. 6881: The appellant, a co sharer in the joint land of the appellant and his brother, was the owner of a piece of land. The appellant sold the land to the respondent, who was the purchaser. The respondent filed a suit for pre emption on the ground that the sale was invalid as it was not made by all the co sharers jointly. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the sale did not amount to an alienation of property within the meaning of section 15(1)(a) of the Punjab Pre emption Act, 1913. On appeal, the High Court held that the sale could be valid only if it was made by all co sharers together. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the sale was void because it was made without the consent of the co sharer; (ii) the sale being voidable under section 15(2), the sale was not valid; (iii) the sale having been made by all members of the family, the sale was bad in law; (iv) the sale had been made by the appellant himself and his brother and (v) the sale could not be said to have been made by any member of the family. HELD: (i) The sale was not made in favour of the appellant alone but was made by the other members of the joint family. [124A] (ii) The sale is not invalid merely because it was effected by all the members of the Joint Hindu Family. The joint family consists of all the members. The joint Hindu family has no separate existence. The joint property of the members of a joint family is not liable to partition unless there are special circumstances which justify such a course. [125B C] (iii) The sale in question was not made with the consent of all the co members of the Hindu family. The sale was made by only one member of the joint Hindu family. [126C D] (iv) The sale having been effected by all members, the joint family cannot be said to be a joint Hindu family and the sale is not void. [127D]

415: The appellant was detained under the Bombay Police Act, 1951, on the grounds that he had been acting in a manner prejudicial to the relations of India with the Portuguese Government and that the police procured the detention order for the purpose of suppressing the freedom of the appellant to ventilate his point of view on the Goan Politics and to take up professionally the cause of persons in the position of Carlos. The grounds of detention were vague and lacking in material particulars. The appellant challenged the validity of the order of detention by a writ petition before the High Court which quashed the order of the detention on the ground that the detaining authority acted merely at the instance of the police who were in league with the Goan Action Committee and that the Police obtained the detention order from the police who could not be expected to know the facts of the case. Held: (i) that the order of preventive detention is not invalid because it does not disclose any real application of mind by the detaining authority. It is a well settled rule of construction that every statute or statutory document must be read as a whole and its language should receive the interpretation interpreted in the light of what is clearly expressed in the Statute itself. In the present case, the grounds of detention do not disclose any such real application of the mind by the Detaining Authority. [385 D] (ii)The order of detention cannot be sustained on the ground of non disclosure of the fact that the detenu had been acting on behalf of the Goan action Committee. The mere fact that the Chief Minister had made an endorsement to the effect that the detenu 's representation had been considered by the Advisory Board would not vitiate the order of his detention. The fact that the Advisory Board had rejected the representation did not make any difference to the question whether the order of bail was proper or not. The order of detention was therefore valid.
